title: Give Your Mind a Target
steps:
DAY 1 — GIVE YOUR MIND A TARGET
THE FOUR-MINUTE WALL
For years, the four-minute mile seemed impossible.
Elite runners chased it.
Coaches studied it.
Athletes got close.
But nobody could break through.
4:01.
4:02.
4:03.
Close enough to believe it might be possible.
Far enough away for four minutes to begin feeling like a wall.
Eventually, that wall became more than a number.
It became a belief.
There was speculation about whether the human body was even capable of running a mile in
under four minutes. And every failed attempt seemed to provide more evidence:
Maybe this is simply the limit.
Then Roger Bannister came along.
Bannister wasn't training with today's technology. He wasn't surrounded by the recovery tools,
sports science, nutrition, and performance facilities modern athletes have access to.
He was a medical student fitting his training around his studies.
But he had something powerful:
A target.
Four minutes.
Not:
"I want to run faster."
Not:
"I want to become a great runner."
Not:
"I want to see how good I can become."
3:59.
That was the target.
On May 6, 1954, Bannister stepped onto the track at Oxford.
The conditions weren't perfect.
The wind was strong enough that Bannister reportedly considered postponing the attempt.
But eventually, the wind began to settle.
He ran.
Lap after lap, his pacemakers pushed the pace.
Bannister entered the final stretch exhausted.
He drove toward the finish line and collapsed shortly after crossing it.
Then came the announcement.
3 minutes, 59.4 seconds.
The wall was gone.
But here's where the story gets even more interesting.
Bannister didn't suddenly change human biology.
He changed what people believed was possible.
Just 46 days later, Australian runner John Landy also broke four minutes.
Eventually, many more runners would do it.
The number that had once represented an impossible barrier became something elite runners
knew could be reached.
The human body hadn't suddenly been redesigned.
The target had become real.
PULL BACK THE CURTAIN
There is an enormous difference between wanting something and targeting something.
Most athletes have wishes.
"I want to get better."
"I want to start."
"I want to play college."
"I want to get stronger."
"I want to hit more."
"I want to have a great season."
There's nothing wrong with those desires.
But your mind can't execute "better."
Better by how much?
By when?
Measured how?
What would need to happen today?
A vague goal produces vague action.
That's why one of the first steps toward becoming a more intentional athlete is learning to give
your mind a specific target.
Imagine walking onto an archery range.
Someone hands you a bow and an arrow.
You get into position.
But there is no target.
They simply tell you:
"Shoot."
Where?
How would you know whether you hit it?
How would you adjust after your first attempt?
How would you measure improvement?
You couldn't.
And yet many athletes are living their athletic careers exactly like this.
They're working.
Training.
Practicing.
Lifting.
Going to lessons.
Playing games.
But if you ask them:
"What exactly are you trying to accomplish over the next 90 days?"
They don't know.
They're shooting arrows without a target.
YOUR MIND NEEDS DIRECTION
Once you choose a clear goal, something interesting begins happening.
You start noticing things connected to it.
If your goal is to become a starter, practices begin looking different.
You start paying attention to what the starter does well.
You notice what your coach rewards.
You recognize weaknesses you previously ignored.
You begin asking different questions.
If your goal is to increase your batting average, suddenly every at-bat contains information.
If your goal is to cut your 40-yard dash time, sleep matters differently.
Nutrition matters differently.
Your first ten yards matter differently.
Your technique matters differently.
If your goal is to earn a college scholarship, today's practice is no longer just another practice.
It's connected to something larger.
Clarity creates relevance.
When you know what you're looking for, you begin seeing things you previously walked right
past.
That's why goals aren't simply about the future.
A great goal changes how you see today.
EVERYTHING HAPPENS THREE TIMES
There's a principle I want you to remember:
Everything happens three times.
First in the mind.
Then on paper.
Then in reality.
Before something can become your reality, you have to be able to see where you're going.
That's the first creation.
Then you take that thought and make it concrete.
You write it down.
That's the second creation.
Eventually, through repeated action, discipline, adjustment, and persistence, you begin creating it
in the physical world.
That's the third creation.
Mind → Paper → Reality.
Most people skip the second step.
They think about what they want.
They talk about what they want.
They tell themselves they'll remember.
Then life happens.
Practice gets difficult.
School gets busy.
They have a bad game.
Motivation drops.
And the goal slowly disappears into the background.
That's why we write.
Writing forces you to take something floating around in your head and give it form.
You can see it.
Read it.
Review it.
Measure yourself against it.
Your goal stops being a thought.
It becomes a target.
FILM ROOM
Take a second and think about your athletic life right now.
Not five years from now.
Not the dream version of your career.
The next 90 days.
If you could make one meaningful improvement or accomplish one meaningful result over the
next 90 days, what would it be?
Don't rush your answer.
And don't write something because it sounds impressive.
This is your target.
Ask yourself:
What do I actually want?
Why does it matter to me?
What would accomplishing it change?
How would I know I achieved it?
Then make it specific.
Instead of:
"I want to get stronger."
Try:
"Over the next 90 days, I will increase my squat from ___ to ___."
Instead of:
"I want to become a better hitter."
Try:
"Over the next 90 days, I will improve my contact rate from ___ to ___."
Instead of:
"I want more playing time."
That may require a different kind of goal because you don't completely control the lineup.
Instead:
"Over the next 90 days, I will become one of the most dependable defenders on my team by
improving ___, ___, and ___."
That's important.
The best goals don't only tell you what you want. They give you something you can pursue.
PRACTICE INSTALL — BUILD YOUR TARGET
Now we're going to create your first 90-Day Goal Card.
But don't enter it into the app yet.
First...
write it down.
Grab your journal, notebook, or an index card.
There is something different about physically sitting with your goal long enough to write it.
At the top of the page write:
MY 90-DAY TARGET
Then complete these:
My Goal:
Over the next 90 days, I will __________________________.
My Deadline:
I will accomplish this by __________________________.
My Measurement:
I will know I'm making progress because __________________________.
My Why:
This matters to me because __________________________.
Don't worry about creating the perfect plan yet.
That's coming.
Today we're establishing the destination.
NOW PUT IT IN THE APP
Once you've written the goal by hand, open the Goals section inside The Complete Athlete.
Enter your 90-day target.
This is important because over the next few days we're going to take that goal and connect it to
something even more powerful:
Your Daily Priorities.
Your goal tells you where you're going.
Your priorities tell you what matters today.
Eventually, we want those two things connected.
Because a goal sitting inside an app won't change your life.
A goal written inside a notebook won't change your life.
Even a perfectly constructed goal won't change your life.
The actions the goal produces will.
And that's where we're going next.
CLOSING THE DAY
Roger Bannister didn't chase "faster."
He chased 3:59.
There was a finish line.
There was a number.
There was something his preparation could organize itself around.
You need the same thing.
Not necessarily a record.
Not necessarily a championship.
Not someone else's definition of success.
Your target.
Because once you know where you're going, we can begin answering the question that separates
people who set goals from people who actually accomplish them:
What must you do today to get there?
Tomorrow, we're going to take the goal you just created and work backward.
Goal → Milestones → Weekly Standards → Daily Priorities.
Because the goal may be 90 days away.
But the work?
The work starts tomorrow.

title: Reverse Engineer the Win
steps:
DAY 2 — REVERSE ENGINEER THE WIN
THE SCOREBOARD PROBLEM
Nick Saban became one of the most successful coaches in the history of college football.
National championships.
Conference championships.
NFL draft picks.
All-Americans.
Teams that entered seasons with enormous expectations.
But one of the most important ideas behind his success had almost nothing to do with thinking
about championships.
In fact, Saban taught his players to stop thinking about the scoreboard.
Stop thinking about the championship.
Stop thinking about the opponent.
Stop thinking about everything that could happen later.
Instead, focus on something much smaller:
The next play.
Saban called this The Process.
The basic philosophy was simple:
Don't become consumed with the final result.
Focus on executing the thing directly in front of you as well as you possibly can.
The next rep.
The next assignment.
The next play.
Do that correctly.
Then do it again.
And again.
And again.
Because championships aren't actually won on championship night.
They are revealed there.
The championship is built months earlier.
In weight rooms.
Film rooms.
Position meetings.
Summer workouts.
Walk-throughs.
Practices nobody watches.
Meals nobody applauds.
Decisions nobody posts online.
By the time everyone sees the trophy...
thousands of smaller decisions have already been made.
That's The Process.
And it's also one of the most important things you can understand about goals.
PULL BACK THE CURTAIN
Yesterday, you created your 90-day target.
That's important.
But now I'm going to tell you something that might sound strange:
Stop staring at it.
You need to know where you're going.
But you cannot spend every day obsessing over the destination.
Imagine your goal is to score 20 goals this season.
You can't wake up tomorrow and:
"Score 20 goals."
That's not an action.
Maybe your goal is to make varsity.
You can't put:
"Make varsity"
on today's to-do list.
Maybe your goal is to gain 10 pounds of muscle.
You can't walk into the gym today and gain 10 pounds of muscle.
The goal tells you where you're going.
But there is still a massive question left unanswered:
What does this goal require from me today?
That is where most goal-setting breaks down.
Athletes create outcomes...
but never translate them into behaviors.
And eventually the goal becomes something they hope happens instead of something they're
actively building.
We're not doing that.
We're going to work backward.
START AT THE FINISH LINE
Take the goal you wrote yesterday.
Imagine that 90 days have passed.
You accomplished it.
Now ask:
What had to happen for this result to become possible?
Let's say your goal is:
"In 90 days, I want to increase my vertical jump by four inches."
Great.
Now work backward.
What would probably have to improve?
Your strength.
Your explosiveness.
Your jumping mechanics.
Your recovery.
Your consistency.
Now go another level deeper.
What would need to happen every week?
Maybe:
3 strength sessions.
2 plyometric sessions.
Mobility work.
Proper recovery.
Consistent sleep.
Now go even deeper.
What would need to happen today?
Maybe today's priority is:
Complete lower-body strength workout.
Now we're getting somewhere.
We just took something 90 days away...
and turned it into something you can do at 4:00 this afternoon.
That's how goals become real.
THE GOAL LADDER
Here's the system I want you to remember:
GOAL → MILESTONES → WEEKLY STANDARDS → DAILY PRIORITIES
Think of it like a ladder.
Your goal is at the top.
You don't jump from the ground to the top.
You climb.
One rung at a time.
1. THE GOAL
Where am I going?
This is the 90-day target you created yesterday.
Example:
Increase my free-throw percentage from 65% to 78%.
2. THE MILESTONES
What would show me I'm moving in the right direction?
Instead of waiting 90 days to discover whether you're improving, create checkpoints.
For example:
Day 30: 69%
Day 60: 74%
Day 90: 78%
Now you can measure progress.
And if you're behind?
You adjust.
That's not failure.
That's information.
3. THE WEEKLY STANDARDS
Now ask:
What must happen consistently each week for those milestones to become realistic?
Maybe:
Shoot 500 intentional free throws.
Complete 3 focused shooting sessions.
Track makes and misses.
Review technique.
Complete visualization work before each session.
These aren't outcomes.
These are standards.
There's a difference.
You can't completely control whether every shot goes in.
But you can control whether you complete the work required to become a better shooter.
4. THE DAILY PRIORITIES
Now we arrive at the most important level.
What needs to happen today?
Not someday.
Not this season.
Not when you're motivated.
Today.
Maybe today's priorities are:
• Make 100 intentional free throws.
• Complete 10 minutes of visualization.
• Record today's shooting percentage.
Those are actions.
Those can be completed.
And when you complete them, something powerful happens:
You win the day.
THE TWO SCOREBOARDS
Most athletes only pay attention to one scoreboard.
The Outcome Scoreboard.
Points.
Hits.
Goals.
Times.
Wins.
Rankings.
Playing time.
Offers.
Statistics.
Those things matter.
But there's another scoreboard that might matter even more:
The Execution Scoreboard.
Did you complete your workout?
Did you get your reps?
Did you watch film?
Did you recover correctly?
Did you complete your priorities?
Did you keep the promises you made to yourself?
One scoreboard measures results.
The other measures behavior.
You don't always control the first.
You have far more control over the second.
And here's the interesting part:
If you consistently win the Execution Scoreboard...
you give yourself a much better chance of eventually winning the Outcome Scoreboard.
That's The Process.
FILM ROOM
Open the goal you created yesterday.
Read it again.
Now ask yourself:
"If I accomplished this goal 90 days from now, what would
probably have to be true?"
Write down everything that comes to mind.
What would you have practiced?
What would you have improved?
What would you have stopped doing?
How often would you have trained?
What habits would you have built?
What sacrifices would you have made?
What would your coach have noticed?
What numbers would have changed?
Don't think about what sounds impressive.
Think about what would actually be required.
Now look at what you wrote.
Somewhere inside those answers is your process.
PRACTICE INSTALL — BUILD YOUR GOAL LADDER
Take out the goal you wrote by hand yesterday.
We're adding to it.
Underneath your goal, write:
MY 90-DAY GOAL
Then:
MY MILESTONES
30-Day Checkpoint:
60-Day Checkpoint:
90-Day Target:
Now write:
MY WEEKLY STANDARDS
What 3–5 things must consistently happen every week?
1.
2.
3.
4.
5.
And finally:
MY DAILY PRIORITIES
Ask yourself:
What are the most important actions I can take TODAY that move me toward this goal?
Choose no more than three.
Priority 1
Priority 2
Priority 3
Notice what we just did.
Yesterday you had a goal.
Today...
you have a path.
NOW OPEN THE APP
Go to your Goal inside The Complete Athlete.
Look at the target you entered yesterday.
Now use your Daily Priorities to connect today's actions to that goal.
This is where I want you to develop a new habit.
Every day, look at your goal and ask:
"What does this goal need from me today?"
Then choose your priorities accordingly.
Your Daily Priorities shouldn't become a giant list of everything you could possibly do.
That's not focus.
Choose the few actions that actually move the needle.
If you have 15 priorities...
you probably don't have priorities.
You have a list.
Your priorities answer one question:
What matters most today?
DON'T CONFUSE MOTION WITH PROGRESS
This is going to become important.
Athletes can be extremely busy without actually moving toward their goals.
You can train for two hours and avoid the weakness you actually need to address.
You can take 300 swings with poor intention.
You can spend an hour in the gym without following a plan.
You can watch motivational videos about becoming great without doing anything greatness
requires.
That's motion.
Progress is different.
Progress has direction.
Remember yesterday:
A goal gives your future a destination and your present a direction.
Your priorities protect that direction.
CLOSING THE DAY
Nick Saban's teams didn't walk into practice and practice winning a national championship.
You can't practice a championship.
You practice the behaviors that make championships possible.
Rep by rep.
Assignment by assignment.
Day by day.
The same is true for your goal.
Your 90-day target may feel far away.
Good.
Leave it there.
Then bring your attention back to where your power actually exists:
Today.
Yesterday, you gave your mind a target.
Today, you built the path.
Tomorrow, we're going deeper.
Because eventually you're going to discover something:
The goal isn't only asking you to DO something.
It's asking you to BECOME someone.
Tomorrow we'll meet that person.
Current You → Required You.

title: Become the Person the Goal Requires
steps:
DAY 3 — BECOME THE PERSON THE GOAL REQUIRES
BEFORE SHOHEI OHTANI BECAME SHOHEI OHTANI
Before the MVP awards.
Before the massive contracts.
Before the home runs that seemed impossible for a pitcher to hit.
Before the strikeouts.
Before becoming one of the most unique players baseball had ever seen...
Shohei Ohtani was a teenager with a piece of paper.
At Hanamaki Higashi High School in Japan, Ohtani had an enormous goal.
He wanted to become a first-round draft pick.
But instead of simply writing:
BECOME A FIRST-ROUND DRAFT PICK
and hoping it happened...

he broke the goal apart.
Ohtani used a goal-setting framework associated with the Harada Method called a mandala
chart.
The structure was simple but powerful.
In the center was the primary goal.
Surrounding that goal were eight areas he believed would help him achieve it.
Things like:
Body building.
Control.
Sharpness.
Speed.
Breaking balls.
Humanity.
Mentality.
And one category that might surprise you:
Luck.
Then he went even deeper.
Each of those eight areas was broken into eight specific actions or behaviors.
One goal.
Eight major areas.
Eight actions underneath each area.
64 pieces surrounding one target.
Suddenly his dream wasn't just something in his imagination.
He could see what it required.

[IMAGE:/plan-covers/goal-blueprint-day-3-photo-1.png|Shohei Ohtani's mandala goal chart]
THE BOX THAT CHANGES EVERYTHING
Here's what makes Ohtani's chart so interesting.
If you looked at it expecting nothing but baseball drills...
you'd be wrong.
Some boxes were about baseball.
Some were about physical development.
Some were about mentality.
But others were about character.
Cleaning his room.
Picking up trash.
Greeting people.
Taking care of equipment.
Reading books.
Being grateful.
Treating people well.
Why would any of that matter if the goal was becoming a great baseball player?
Because Ohtani and his coaches understood something deeper:
The goal wasn't only going to require better baseball skills.
It was going to require a better Shohei.
The player and the person couldn't be separated.
His goal wasn't simply asking:
"How good can you throw?"
It was also asking:
"Who must you become?"
PULL BACK THE CURTAIN
Yesterday we built:
GOAL → MILESTONES → WEEKLY STANDARDS → DAILY PRIORITIES
Today we're going deeper.
Because sometimes athletes look at a goal and immediately ask:
"What do I need to do?"
That's a good question.
But there's an even better one:
"Who do I need to become?"
Imagine your goal is to earn a college scholarship.
What does that version of you look like?
More disciplined?
Stronger?
More coachable?
Better academically?
More consistent?
More confident?
A better teammate?
More responsible?
More intentional about recovery?
Maybe your goal is becoming a starter.
What would a coach need to see before trusting you with that responsibility?
Maybe your goal is dropping your 40 time.
What kind of athlete follows the training plan long enough to make that happen?
Maybe your goal is improving your batting average.
What kind of hitter studies their at-bats, controls emotions after failure, gets extra reps, and
attacks weaknesses?
Every goal has requirements.
Some are physical.
Some are technical.
Some are mental.
Some are behavioral.
Some are personal.
That's what Ohtani's boxes exposed.
YOUR GOAL HAS HIDDEN REQUIREMENTS
Go back to the 90-day goal you wrote on Day 1.
Look at it again.
Now imagine your goal sitting in the center of a page.
Around it are empty boxes.
Your job is to answer:
What areas of my life and performance must improve for
this goal to become more likely?
Maybe it's:
Skill
Strength
Speed
Nutrition
Recovery
Confidence
Discipline
Leadership
Your eight categories might be completely different.
That's okay.
This is your goal.
But here's where this exercise becomes powerful.
We're not stopping at the categories.
We're going underneath them.
THE OHTANI METHOD
Let's say your goal is:
MAKE VARSITY
You might decide eight areas matter:
1. Skill
2. Strength
3. Speed
4. Game IQ
5. Confidence
6. Recovery
7. Coachability
8. Character
Now take Skill.
What actually improves your skill?
Maybe:
Extra reps.
Weak-side work.
Position-specific drills.
Film study.
Private training.
Fundamentals.
Game-speed reps.
Tracking weaknesses.
Those become your boxes.
Now take Confidence.
Maybe:
Positive self-talk.
Visualization.
Preparation.
Reviewing previous wins.
Body language.
Reset routine.
Doing uncomfortable things.
Keeping promises to yourself.
Another eight boxes.
Suddenly...
MAKE VARSITY
isn't just a dream anymore.
You're beginning to see the athlete capable of making varsity.
CURRENT YOU VS. REQUIRED YOU
This is where I want you to be extremely honest.
There is a version of you who exists today.
CURRENT YOU.
And there is a version of you capable of accomplishing the goal you wrote.
REQUIRED YOU.
There may be a gap between them.
Good.
Don't be embarrassed by the gap.
Study it.
Maybe Current You avoids weaknesses.
Required You attacks them.
Maybe Current You trains when motivated.
Required You follows the schedule.
Maybe Current You gets defensive when corrected.
Required You seeks coaching.
Maybe Current You stays up too late.
Required You protects recovery.
Maybe Current You loses confidence after mistakes.
Required You resets quickly.
Your goal is showing you where you need to grow.
That's one of the greatest purposes goals serve.
THE MOST IMPORTANT PART OF OHTANI'S CHART
It would be easy to look at Ohtani's chart and think the magic was the 64 boxes.
It wasn't.
You could fill out 640 boxes and accomplish nothing.
The chart didn't make Shohei Ohtani great.
The chart gave his work direction.
He still had to train.
He still had to lift.
He still had to practice.
He still had to develop.
He still had to make decisions every day that matched the athlete he wanted to become.
That's why yesterday's lesson matters so much.
Eventually every box has to find its way into:
TODAY.
A goal chart that never changes your behavior is just decorated paper.
FILM ROOM — BUILD YOUR 8
Take out the Goal Card you've been building.
At the top of a new page, write your 90-day goal.
Circle it.
Now ask:
"What eight areas would make me more capable of
accomplishing this goal?"
Write eight.
MY TARGET
________________________________
MY 8
1. ______________________________
2. ______________________________
3. ______________________________
4. ______________________________
5. ______________________________
6. ______________________________
7. ______________________________
8. ______________________________
Don't just think about your sport.
Think about the whole athlete.
Your body.
Your mind.
Your habits.
Your preparation.
Your character.
Your recovery.
Your relationships.
Your discipline.
Your goal might require improvement somewhere you haven't been looking.
PRACTICE INSTALL — GO FROM 8 TO 64
Now we're going to do what Ohtani did.
Take each of your eight categories.
Underneath it, identify eight behaviors, habits, skills, or actions that would improve that area.
Eight categories.
Eight actions each.
8 × 8 = 64.
Don't rush this.
This isn't an exercise you need to finish in five minutes.
Write it down by hand.
Sit with it.
Think.
Ask yourself:
What would actually move this area forward?
What am I currently avoiding?
What does Required Me do that Current Me doesn't?
By the time you're finished, you should be able to look at that piece of paper and see something
powerful:
Not just what you want.
Who your goal requires you to become.
NOW CONNECT IT TO THE APP
Here's where we're going to make your chart useful.
Look at your 64 boxes.
You are not going to try doing all 64 today.
That's not discipline.
That's chaos.
Instead, your chart becomes a menu.
Your goal determines the direction.
Your chart identifies the behaviors.
And your Daily Priorities determine today's work.
Each day, ask:
"Which actions from my goal chart matter most today?"
Then put those actions into your Daily Priorities inside The Complete Athlete.
Maybe today's priority comes from Strength.
Tomorrow's might come from Skill.
Another might come from Recovery.
Another might come from Mentality.
But they all point toward the same target.
Now the system connects:
GOAL
↓
8 DEVELOPMENT AREAS
↓
64 ACTIONS
↓
DAILY PRIORITIES
↓
EXECUTION
This is how something written on paper begins turning into reality.
DON'T JUST CHASE THE ATHLETE
There's one more lesson hidden inside Ohtani's chart.
Remember those boxes about gratitude?
Cleaning?
Respect?
Taking care of equipment?
Those aren't pitching mechanics.
They're not hitting drills.
They're about the person.
That's worth paying attention to.
Because athletics has a way of convincing us that performance is everything.
But becoming a Complete Athlete means developing more than your game.
The goal isn't simply:
Become a better player.
It's also:
Become someone capable of handling becoming a better player.
More disciplined.
More responsible.
More grateful.
More humble.
More coachable.
More dependable.
Better athlete.
Better person.
Complete Athlete.
CLOSING THE DAY
Years before the world knew Shohei Ohtani as an MVP...
a teenager sat down and put his future on paper.
There was a goal in the middle.
And surrounding that goal was a roadmap.
Skills.
Habits.
Mentality.
Character.
Work.
Growth.
He didn't simply write what he wanted.
He studied what it would require.
Now you've done the same.
Three days ago, your goal was an idea.
Then you wrote it down.
Then you built the process.
Today you identified the athlete capable of accomplishing it.
Your Goal Card now contains:
Your 90-Day Target.
Your Milestones.
Your Weekly Standards.
Your Daily Priorities.
Your 8 Development Areas.
Your 64 Actions.
You're no longer staring at a wish.
You're looking at a blueprint.
But there's one final problem we need to solve.
Because goals are easy to write when you're motivated.
They're harder to remember when you're tired.
When you lose.
When progress slows down.
When life gets busy.
When the excitement disappears.
Tomorrow we're going to build the system that keeps your goal alive after the feeling that created
it is gone.
Remember:
Everything happens three times.
First in the mind.
Then on paper.
Then in reality.
Tomorrow...
we start turning the paper into proof.

title: Keep the Target Alive
steps:
DAY 4 — KEEP THE TARGET ALIVE
BRUCE LEE WROTE IT DOWN
Long before Bruce Lee became a global icon, he wrote down a vision for his future.
Not a vague idea.
Not:
"I hope I become successful."
He put his ambition on paper.
In 1969, Lee wrote what has become known as his Definite Chief Aim.
He described the level of success he intended to reach, the value he intended to provide, and
even put a timeline around his vision.
At the time, the future he described wasn't his reality yet.
It existed first...
in his mind.
Then he did something important.
He put it...
on paper.
Years later, Bruce Lee would become one of the most recognizable martial artists and cultural
figures in the world.
But before millions of people could see the vision...
Bruce could.
And before the world experienced it...
he wrote it down.
EVERYTHING HAPPENS THREE TIMES
Over the last four days, we've returned to one principle:
Everything happens three times.
First in the mind.
You see the possibility.
Then on paper.
You define it.
Then in reality.
You build it.
Most athletes spend almost all their time thinking about the third creation.
They want the result.
The starting position.
The scholarship.
The championship.
The faster time.
The improved stats.
But reality is usually the last place the goal appears.
Before you hold it...
you have to see it.
Before you achieve it...
you have to define it.
And once you've defined it...
you have to repeatedly act on it.
That's why writing your goals isn't the finish line.
It's the beginning.
THE GOAL YOU FORGOT
Think about January.
Millions of people set goals.
They buy notebooks.
Create plans.
Write resolutions.
They're excited.
They're focused.
They're motivated.
Then February comes.
Then March.
Life gets busy.
The notebook gets closed.
The routine disappears.
And eventually, the goal that once felt incredibly important becomes something they barely think
about.
The problem wasn't always that the goal was bad.
Sometimes...
they simply stopped looking at it.
What you repeatedly place in front of your mind has a better chance of influencing your
decisions.
That's why your goal cannot live somewhere you visit once every three months.
It needs to stay visible.
Because every day you're making decisions.
Train or don't train.
Extra reps or go home.
Prepare or wing it.
Recover or stay up.
Respond to coaching or get defensive.
Do the priority or procrastinate.
And your future is being built through those seemingly small decisions.
PULL BACK THE CURTAIN
There's something you need to understand about motivation.
It changes.
Some days you'll feel unstoppable.
Other days you won't.
There will be days when your goal feels close.
There will be days when it feels incredibly far away.
There will be great games.
Bad games.
Breakthroughs.
Plateaus.
Compliments.
Criticism.
Progress.
Setbacks.
That's normal.
Which is exactly why your goal system cannot depend on:
"Do I feel motivated today?"
You need something stronger.
A REVIEW SYSTEM.
The purpose of reviewing your goals isn't to hype yourself up every morning.
It's to remind yourself:
This is where I'm going.
This is why it matters.
This is who I'm becoming.
And this is what matters today.
THE GOAL LOOP
Over the last four days, you've built almost everything you need.
Now we're going to put it together.
Your system looks like this:
WRITE → REVIEW → PRIORITIZE → EXECUTE → MEASURE → ADJUST → REPEAT
Let's break it down.
1. WRITE
Your goal begins on paper.
Not just in your head.
Write exactly what you're pursuing.
Writing creates clarity.
You did this on Day 1.
2. REVIEW
Keep the target in front of you.
Read your goal regularly.
Look at your Goal Card.
Remember why you started.
Review the person you're becoming.
Your goal shouldn't surprise you when you see it again.
You should know it.
3. PRIORITIZE
Now ask:
"What does this goal need from me today?"
Not everything.
The most important things.
Use the Daily Priorities inside The Complete Athlete to identify the actions that deserve your
attention today.
Your goal determines your direction.
Your priorities determine today's focus.
4. EXECUTE
Then stop planning.
Do the work.
This sounds obvious.
But athletes can become addicted to preparation without execution.
Making schedules feels productive.
Writing goals feels productive.
Watching motivational content feels productive.
Creating Ohtani charts feels productive.
But eventually...
you have to take the swing.
Run the sprint.
Lift the weight.
Watch the film.
Complete the recovery.
Have the conversation.
Do the rep.
The goal moves when you move.
5. MEASURE
Remember the milestones you created on Day 2?
Use them.
Numbers tell the truth.
Maybe you're improving faster than expected.
Maybe you're behind.
Maybe one part of the plan isn't working.
Good.
Now you have information.
Don't be afraid of the scoreboard.
Use it.
6. ADJUST
This might be one of the most important parts.
Your plan is allowed to change.
Your commitment doesn't have to.
If something isn't working...
adjust.
If you've improved faster than expected...
adjust.
If your coach gives you new information...
adjust.
If circumstances change...
adjust.
Changing the strategy doesn't mean you're quitting the goal.
A GPS doesn't throw away the destination because you missed a turn.
It finds another route.
Do the same.
7. REPEAT
This is where goals are actually achieved.
Not through one incredible day.
Through enough ordinary days pointed in the same direction.
Review.
Prioritize.
Execute.
Measure.
Adjust.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Until eventually...
what was once written on paper becomes something you're living.
YOUR DAILY GOAL ROUTINE
Let's make this ridiculously practical.
Every morning—or before you begin your athletic work—take two minutes.
Open your Goals section inside The Complete Athlete.
Read your 90-day target.
Then ask:
"What does this goal need from me today?"
Look at the Goal Card you created.
Look at your weekly standards.
Look at your Ohtani-style development areas.
Then choose your Daily Priorities.
That's it.
You don't need a 45-minute morning routine.
You need clarity.
Goal → Today.
Then go execute.
YOUR WEEKLY RESET
Once each week, go deeper.
Take out the Goal Card you physically wrote.
Yes...
the paper one.
Review it.
Then answer four questions:
1. WHAT DID I SAY I WOULD DO?
Look at your weekly standards.
2. WHAT DID I ACTUALLY DO?
No excuses.
No judgment.
Just truth.
3. WHAT'S WORKING?
Identify the behaviors producing progress.
Keep them.
4. WHAT NEEDS TO CHANGE?
Identify where you're falling short.
Then adjust next week's priorities.
This prevents you from spending 90 days following a plan that isn't working.
Great athletes don't only work hard.
They pay attention.
PRACTICE INSTALL — COMPLETE YOUR 90-DAY GOAL CARD
You've been building this for four days.
Now it's time to finish it.
Take out your handwritten Goal Card.
It should now contain:
MY 90-DAY TARGET
What exactly am I pursuing?
MY DEADLINE
When will I accomplish it?
MY WHY
Why does this matter to me?
MY MILESTONES
30 Days: ____________________
60 Days: ____________________
90 Days: ____________________
MY WEEKLY STANDARDS
What must consistently happen each week?
MY 8 DEVELOPMENT AREAS
What areas must improve?
MY 64 ACTIONS
Your eight actions underneath each development area.
THE PERSON I MUST BECOME
What qualities does this goal require?
MY DAILY PRIORITIES
What matters most today?
PUT THE SYSTEM TO WORK
Now open The Complete Athlete.
Make sure your 90-day target is inside your Goals section.
Then connect today's actions to your Daily Priorities.
From this point forward, those two features should work together.
Your Goals section answers:
"Where am I going?"
Your Daily Priorities answer:
"What am I doing about it today?"
That's the relationship.
Your goal should influence your priorities.
And your priorities should move you toward your goal.
Future → Present.
Vision → Action.
Goal → Today.
DON'T DIG UP THE SEED
There's one final thing you need to understand.
Progress isn't always obvious.
You can work for weeks and feel like nothing is happening.
Then suddenly...
something clicks.
You get stronger.
Your timing improves.
The game slows down.
Your confidence changes.
Your coach notices.
The opportunity comes.
That's why you can't keep digging up the seed to see if it's growing.
Plant.
Water.
Work.
Measure.
Adjust.
Keep going.
Your responsibility is not to force tomorrow's result.
Your responsibility is to make today's deposit.
Then make another tomorrow.
CLOSING THE PLAN — FROM PAPER TO PROOF
Four days ago, you started with an idea.
Something you wanted.
Maybe something you've wanted for a long time.
But we refused to leave it there.
DAY 1 — YOU DEFINED THE TARGET.
You stopped saying:
"I want to get better."
And decided what better actually means.
You wrote it down.
DAY 2 — YOU BUILT THE PATH.
You took something 90 days away and worked backward.
Goal → Milestones → Weekly Standards → Daily Priorities.
You learned that the goal isn't your daily job.
Today's responsibility is.
DAY 3 — YOU BUILT THE ATHLETE.
Shohei Ohtani showed us that extraordinary goals have requirements.
You identified your development areas.
You created your actions.
And you asked one of the most important questions an athlete can ask:
"Who must I become?"
DAY 4 — YOU BUILT THE SYSTEM.
Write.
Review.
Prioritize.
Execute.
Measure.
Adjust.
Repeat.
Now you have more than a goal.
You have an operating system for achieving one.
But remember something.
None of this guarantees the outcome.
Sports don't work that way.
You can do everything right and still encounter injuries, competition, coaching decisions, bad
breaks, and circumstances outside your control.
Goals aren't about controlling the future.
They're about becoming intentional with what you can control today.
And that's why the greatest thing these next 90 days may produce isn't the number you wrote at
the top of your Goal Card.
It might be you.
More disciplined.
More focused.
More confident.
More intentional.
More consistent.
More accountable.
A better competitor.
A better teammate.
A more complete athlete.
So keep the card.
Keep writing.
Keep reviewing.
Keep using your Goals.
Keep setting your Daily Priorities.
And keep making deposits.
Because eventually, if you do this long enough, something incredible can happen.
You look back at the piece of paper you once wrote your future on...
and realize you're standing inside something that used to exist only in your imagination.
Remember:
EVERYTHING HAPPENS THREE TIMES.
First in the mind.
See it.
Then on paper.
Define it.
Then in reality.
Build it.
One goal.
One priority.
One day.
One deposit at a time.
Now go make it real.
